analysis.one_liner: Bans top ex-officials and ex-lawmakers from lobbying Congress or agencies for one year.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced March 2, 1994 with 5 cosponsors, it sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee until the Congress ended on January 3, 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added a one-year "cooling off" period: after leaving office, the President, Vice President, top executive appointees, Members of Congress, and congressional staff making $110,000 or more could not lobby their former colleagues, nor supervise anyone else who lobbies, for a year. It tightened existing federal law, which mostly restricts what former officials can do about specific matters they worked on, by barring them from influence-peddling generally. It was sent to a House subcommittee and never came out.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens get a cleaner government: for one year after leaving, the most senior officials could not immediately cash in their contacts by lobbying Congress or the executive branch, and agencies would face fewer ex-officials pressing their former colleagues' doors. Current lawmakers and executive staff would also face a former colleague arriving as a hired advocate slightly less often.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Citizens who want the revolving door slowed

how_it_helps.text: It bars the President, Vice President, the highest-level executive appointees, and senior Executive Office staff from lobbying any Member or employee of Congress for one year after they leave, and from supervising anyone else who does that lobbying during the same year.

It applies the same one-year ban to Members of Congress, elected officers of each House, and congressional employees paid $110,000 or more, barring them from lobbying the President, the Vice President, or any executive agency on someone else's behalf.

It closes the easiest workaround by also forbidding the barred former officials from holding a supervisory position over people likely to make those lobbying contacts, so they cannot simply be the boss behind the scenes.
The bill also covers mid-level political appointees (noncareer appointees earning $110,000 or more), so the restriction is not limited only to cabinet-rank officials.

analysis.who_pays: Former senior officials and lobbying firms would lose the ability to put a freshly departed cabinet secretary, lawmaker, or senior staffer on the payroll and immediately have them lobby their old colleagues. No taxpayer money is involved; the cost is borne by the officials who would have to wait a year to sell their contacts, and by the industries that hire them.

drawbacks.text: The cooling-off period lasts only one year, so a former official could still begin lobbying the very next year; the bill slows the revolving door but does not close it.

The ban turns on the former official 'knowingly' acting 'with intent to influence,' a standard that is hard to prove and easy to design around, for example by advising a lobbying colleague informally.

The bill as drafted is internally inconsistent: the legislative-branch section restricts lobbying contacts for one year but then says the supervisory ban lasts 'a 2-year period,' a drafting error that would have created confusion about which term applies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain is real but modest: a one-year pause on the most senior officials turning their contacts into lobbying income, with the supervisory ban closing the most obvious loophole. Against that, the bill covers only the top tiers of government, expires quickly, and relies on an intent standard that is difficult to enforce, and its text contains a drafting error. It would have been a step toward slower revolving doors, not a solution to them.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to a House Judiciary subcommittee two days after introduction and never moved again; the bill died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Dick Zimmer and Rep. Buddy Bacchus introduced the Revolving Door Reform Act on March 2, 1994, to tighten the federal rules on former executive and legislative branch officials.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never brought it up.
On March 4, 1994 it was referred further down to the Subcommittee on Administrative Law and Governmental Relations, where it stayed.
No hearing, markup, or vote is recorded; the bill remained in subcommittee until the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, at which point it expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lobbying firms and the former officials they hire came out ahead: the rules stayed exactly as loose as before, and senior ex-officials kept the right to lobby their former colleagues the day after leaving office.

for.name: Rep. Dick Zimmer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Revolving Door Reform Act on March 2, 1994 to tighten lobbying restrictions on former officials.

for.name: Rep. Buddy Bacchus
for.what_they_did: Joined Zimmer in introducing the bill at its introduction.

against.name: Rep. Jack Brooks
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on March 2, 1994 and never scheduled it for a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

against.name: House Judiciary Subcommittee on Administrative Law and Governmental Relations
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from March 4, 1994 onward and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsored the bill with 1 Democratic and 4 Republican cosponsors, and it died in a Democratic-controlled committee without anyone ever voting against it on the merits.

industries.note: The bill would have cut off their fastest hiring pipeline: newly departed cabinet secretaries, lawmakers, and $110,000-plus staffers could not lobby for a year, or even supervise lobbying during that year. Firms would have had to wait or hire people with weaker connections.

industries.industry: Corporations and trade groups that hire former officials as advocates
industries.note: Companies that buy access through former policymakers would have lost immediate use of their star hires, since the newest ex-officials could not appear before Congress or agencies on their behalf for a year.

The people who leave government with the most valuable contacts are precisely whom the bill restricts; it would have delayed by one year their ability to monetize their service, whether in-house at a company or at a lobbying firm.
